Xiaogang Luo[⁎](#_bookmark0), Liming Liu, Langrun Wang, Xiaoteng Liu, Yixin Cai

_School of Chemical Engineering and Pharmacy, Wuhan Institute of Technology, Wuhan, 430073, China_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Chitosan/cellulose nanocomposite microspheres

Activated carbon Tylosin

Column adsorption Adsorption mechanism

A B S T R A C T

Antibiotic pollution in tap water, surface water, and eﬄuent needs to be controlled in China. Adsorption is an economical and eco-friendly way to solve the antibiotic contamination problem, such as tylosin. In this study, the chitosan/cellulose nanocomposite adsorbents entrapped with activated carbon are prepared by a sol-gel phase inversion method. Structures and properties of the adsorbents are characterized by SEM, EDXS, BET, XRD, FTIR XPS and Zeta potentials. The adsorption behavior of CCM-AC on tylosin is determined by batch and fixed-bed adsorption experiments, while their adsorption mechanism is also studied. The maximum adsorption ca-pacity is 59.26 mg g−1, while the adsorption behavior is in accordance with the Langmuir equation and pseudo-second-order kinetics. These results confirm that the tylosin adsorption process is affected by chemical and

physical interactions, and the adsorbent can be captured by tylosin with H-bond, electrostatic and π-π electron-

donor-acceptor interaction. Adsorption experiments are significantly affected by pH.

1. Introduction

Tylosin (TYL), one of the most commonly used veterinary antibiotic, has been shown to promote animal growth and is widely used as a therapeutic substance in the treatment of mycoplasmosis in poultry and livestock ([Devreese et al., 2012](#_bookmark17); [Kline & Pinckney, 2016](#_bookmark25)). Un-fortunately, 50%–80% of TYL is excreted into the environment ([Guo,](#_bookmark22) [Yin, Yang, & Dang, 2018](#_bookmark22)) and found in China's surface water, waste-water and soil. Accumulated TYL could induce genetic exchange, in-crease the resistance of bacteria to drugs, and have a potentially ne-gative impact on aquatic ecosystems and human health ([Yao et al.,](#_bookmark41) [2017](#_bookmark41)). Therefore, removal of low concentrations of TYL in the water is of great significance for water condition and ecological environment protection.

TYL is composed of a 16-membered polyketide lactone ring and three 6-deoxyhexose sugars: mycaminose, mycinose and mycarose ([Chopra, Van Schepdael, Hoogmartens, & Adams, 2013](#_bookmark14)), they all have one tertiary amine (cation), five hydroxyl groups, and three carbonyl groups. As an ionic compound, TYL has different forms at different pH conditions ([Guo et al., 2016](#_bookmark20)). TYL molecules can be captured by ad-sorbents by different interactions such as Van Der Waals forces, hy-

drophobicity ([Ji, Liu, Xu, Zheng, & Zhu, 2010](#_bookmark24)), π-π electron-donor-

acceptor (EDA) interactions, and/or cation-π interactions ([Fu, Yang,](#_bookmark18) [Wan, Xu, & Zhu, 2011](#_bookmark18)), H-bonds, cation exchange ([ter Laak, Wouter, &](#_bookmark37)

[Tolls, 2010](#_bookmark37)) and surface complexation ([Guo et al., 2013](#_bookmark21)), it is a complex process. These researches are primarily used to assess the adsorption behavior of TYL in the environment, however, there are few reports on TYL removal from slightly polluted water ([Guo et al., 2018](#_bookmark22)). Adsorption is an important method to control the transport and ecological risk of TYL in the environment. Comprehensive understanding of the adsorp-tion mechanism is beneficial to design the adsorbent for TYL removal. Activated carbon (AC) is an attractive option to remove organic contaminants from water. [Guo et al. (2016)](#_bookmark20) used different sources of black carbon to adsorb TYL. However, AC is diﬃcult to separate from the aqueous phase after interaction with the adsorbate, and is likely to cause secondary pollution ([Danalıoğlu, Bayazit, Kerkez Kuyumcu, &](#_bookmark15) [Salam, 2017](#_bookmark15)). Encapsulating AC in bioresource materials can improve the application performance, turning the adsorption process into a

highly eﬃcient and environmentally friendly process.

Chitosan is a non-toxic natural polymer formed by deacetylation of chitin ([Thakur & Thakur, 2014](#_bookmark38)). The amine and hydroxyl groups on the chitosan are capable of adsorbing contaminants through several me-chanisms including chemical interactions and electrostatic interactions ([Hydari, Sharififard, Nabavinia, & Parvizi, 2012](#_bookmark23)). [Du et al. (2018)](#_bookmark19) successfully used modified chitosan to treat TYL in water. The cellulose molecular chain has a large number of hydroxyl groups, and the in-termolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding between these hy-droxyl groups makes the cellulose have a strong rigid structure, and is

suitable for using as a biological aﬃnity carrier. Concurrently, they can adsorb organic contaminants by coupling between cellulose hydroxyl groups and antibiotics ([Luo, Zeng, Liu, & Zhang, 2015](#_bookmark32)).

In this study, combination of AC and chitosan to cellulose may de-sign new nanocomposite adsorbents which possess high adsorption capacity for TYL (10 mg L−1) removal. The nanocomposite adsorbent was prepared by a sol-gel phase inversion method, and the morpholo-gies, structures, physicochemical properties, modification process and adsorption mechanism of the adsorbents were investigated.

1. Experimental section
    1. _Materials_

Cotton linter pulp (ɑ-cellulose > 95%) was supplied by Hubei Chemical Fiber Group Ltd. (Xiangfan, China). Its viscosity-average molecular weight (Mη) was 12.5 × 104 Dalton ([Cai, Liu, & Zhang,](#_bookmark11) [2006](#_bookmark11)). Chitosan (Mw = 100 kDa; degree of deacetylation = 90%) was

provided by Zhejiang Golden-Shell Biochemical Co., China. Activated carbon (AC, C3345) powders were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. TYL was provided by Shandong Lukang Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.

- 1.  _Preparation of CCM-AC_

Chitosan/cellulose nanocomposite microspheres embedded with AC (CCM-AC) were prepared by a sol-gel phase inversion method. 6 wt% cellulose and 6 wt% chitosan solution were prepared as our previous work ([Luo et al., 2017](#_bookmark31)). The chitosan solution and the cellulose solution were mixed in a mass ratio of 5% to obtain a mixed solution a. 2 g of AC was added to the mixed solution, vigorously stirred for 15 min, then centrifuged in a centrifuge to obtain a mixed solution b. First, 12 g of span 80 were added to a three-necked flask containing 500 mL of liquid paraﬃn and stirred at 300 rpm for 1 h. Then, while maintaining the rotation speed, 120 mL of the solution b were added to the three-necked flask. After stirring for two hours, the pH of the mixture was adjusted to

7.0 using 3 M HCL solution, the CCM-AC was formed. The supernatant of the suspended layer after standing and stratified was washed with water and recovered, and the lower aqueous phase was washed three times with deionized water and ethanol, respectively, to remove re-sidual organic leftovers. Pure cellulose microspheres and chitosan/cel-lulose microspheres were coded as CM and CCM, respectively.

- 1.  _Characterization_

The microscopic features of the microsphere samples were char-acterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss SIGMA, Zeiss), and the surface elements were analyzed by energy dis-persive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS, JSM-5510LV). The specific surface area and average pore diameter of the samples were obtained by ni-trogen gas adsorption analyzer (ASAP-2010). The physical properties of the microsphere samples were characterized by pycnometer method ([Luo et al., 2015](#_bookmark32)). The materials were milled to powder and dried under vacuum at 60 °C for 72 h for characterization. The crystal structure of the materials was analyzed by X-ray diffractometer (X’Pert-PRO, Mal-vern Panalytical). The chemical structure and surface chemical state of the sample were determined by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Nicolet 6700, Thermo) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB250Xi, Thermo). The Zeta potential of the samples were determined by Malvern nanoparticle size potentiometer (Zetasizer Nano S90).

- 1.  _Batch adsorption experiments_

In the batch adsorption experiments, effects of the amount of CCM-AC (0.03–0.6 g) and the pH of the solution (3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0 and 11.0) on the adsorption of CCM-AC were investigated. CCM-AC was added to

a series of Erlenmeyer flasks (100 mL) containing 50 mL of TYL solu-tions (10 mg L−1), then the Erlenmeyer flasks were maintained at 298 K and shaken at 200 rpm for 24 h. NaOH or HCl solutions were used for pH adjustment. The nanocomposite adsorbent which adsorbed TYL was encoded as CCM-AC-T.

The kinetic study of TYL adsorption was performed in a reactor equipped with 300 mL of TYL solution (10 mg L−1) and an equal pro-portion of adsorbent. 1.5 mL of the aliquots was taken at the indicated time points for testing.

The isotherm study of TYL adsorption was carried out in a reactor equipped with 50 mL of TYL solution and an equal proportion of ad-sorbent. The concentration of the TYL solution was selected to be 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 mg L−1, The temperature of adsorption process was controlled at 298, 303 and 313 K, respectively.

- 1.  _Fixed-bed column adsorption experiments_

The experimental methods and the processes were carried out ac-cording to our previous work ([Luo et al., 2017](#_bookmark31)). Breakthrough curves were used to investigate the effects of different experimental para-meters such as bed height (2, 3 and 5 cm), flow rate (4, 5 and 6 mL min−1), initial concentration (5, 10 and 15 mg L−1), and pH (3, 7 and 11) on column adsorption experiments. The data were fitted and ana-lyzed using Adams-Bohart ([Bohart & Adams, 1920](#_bookmark12)), Thomas ([Thomas,](#_bookmark39) [1944](#_bookmark39)), Yoon-Nelson ([Yoon & Nelson, 1984](#_bookmark42)), BDST ([Saatçi & Oulman,](#_bookmark35) [1980](#_bookmark35)) and Dose Response ([Yan, Viraraghavan, & Chen, 2001](#_bookmark40)) models. These models are shown in Table S1. The regeneration ability of CCM-AC was studied by using 0.1 M HCl solution as the desorption solution.

1. Results and discussion
    1. _Morphology and structure characterization_

SEM images of CCM-AC and CCM-AC-T are shown in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark1). The microspheres have a regular spherical structure ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark1)a, d), and the particle size of the microspheres is 282.28 ± 59.62 μm by using Image J software. The micro-nano-pore structures can be observed in the surface and interface of the microspheres ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark1)b, e). The porous net-

work structure can not only prevent the loss of AC particles to a certain extent, but also facilitate the diffusion of antibiotics and provide a larger contact area to promote antibiotic adsorption. The element type and content on the CCM-AC and CCM-AC-T surfaces were examined by EDXS patterns ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark1)c, f). Compared with CCM-AC, the contents of O and N atom in CCM-AC-T decreased from 29.68 Ar% and 1.96 Ar% to

28.77 Ar% and 0.56 Ar%, respectively, and the atomic content of C increased from 68.36 Ar% to 70.67 Ar%, indicating that TYL was in-troduced into CCM-AC, confirming the adsorption performances of TYL. Table S2 lists the physical properties of CM, CCM and CCM-AC. The adding of AC leads to the microspheres have more microporous and mesoporous structures. Multi-layered pore structure ensures CCM-AC a high specific surface area (_SBET_), which results in a high liquid absor-bency (over 90%). CCM-AC's high-water content, high porosity and high _SBET_ help to enhance its adsorption capacity, which makes CCM-AC an idea material for treat antibiotic contaminants in water.

Moreover, the _SBET_ of the CCM-AC decreased by 31%, confirming that the microspheres have an adsorption effect on TYL.

XRD patterns of CCM-AC, CCM, CM, AC, native cellulose and chit-osan are shown in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark2)(1). The broad peak at 2θ of 24° for AC in-dicates the presence of an ordered graphite structure. The spectrum curves of the AC are smooth, with no obvious peaks, which may be

advantageous for the sorption of TYL ([Chen, Zhou, & Lin, 2015](#_bookmark13)). The presence of characteristic diffraction peaks of AC in the spectrum of CCM-AC indicates that the filler has been successfully incorporated into the composite.

[Fig. 2](#_bookmark2)(2) indicates the FTIR spectra of CCM-AC, CCM, CM, AC, na-tive cellulose and chitosan, respectively. The spectrum of AC indicates

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 1. SEM images of CCM-AC (a, b) and CCM-AC-T (d, e). EDXS pattern and Particle size (insets) of CCM-AC (c) and CCM-AC-T (f).

that the peak at 1638 cm−1 is the carboxyl vibration peak of carboxylic acid, and the small peak at 400–700 cm−1 may be the out-of-plane bending of CeH in benzene derivative, which is very common in acti-vated carbon ([Mohammadi, Hassani, Mohamed, & Najafpour, 2010](#_bookmark33)). The peak width of CCM-AC at 3340–3420 cm−1 shifted toward high wavenumbers ([Luo et al., 2015](#_bookmark32)). The results show that the amount of intermolecular hydrogen bonds increase, indicating that there is a strong interaction between cellulose, chitosan, and activated carbon.

[Fig. 3](#_bookmark3) shows XPS spectra of a, CM, b, CCM, c, CCM-AC, and d, CCM-AC-T in C 1s, respectively. [Fig. 3](#_bookmark3)a shows the C 1s peak spectrum of CM. The peak at 284.36 eV is caused by CeOH, the strong peak at 284.60 eV is caused by CeC/C\]C, and the peak at 287.76 eV is attributed to OeCeO. The C 1s spectrum of CCM ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark3)b) is basically the same as that of CM, which is consistent with the results of FTIR spectra because cellulose and chitosan have similar macromolecular structures. [Fig. 3](#_bookmark3)c shows the C 1s peak spectrum of CCM-AC. It shows four peaks at

284.11 eV, 286.42 eV, 287.84 eV, and 288.47 eV, which are caused by C\]C/CeC, CeOH, OeCeO and carboxylic acid/ester bond, respec-tively ([Puziy, Poddubnaya, Socha, Gurgul, & Wisniewski, 2008](#_bookmark34)). Be-cause of the embedding of AC, there is one more carboxy peak than [Fig. 3](#_bookmark3)a and b. The carboxy peaks and high-intensity hydroxy peaks appearing in the spectra confirm that the CCM-AC adsorbent has a rich active site, which is favorable for the adsorption of TYL.

[Fig. 3](#_bookmark3)d shows the C 1s peak spectrum of CCM-AC-T. The peak at 287 eV, 287.92 eV, 288.7 eV indicate the OeCeO bond, the ketone group, carboxylic acid/ester bond, respectively ([Li, Du, Deng, Zhu, &](#_bookmark26) [Zhang, 2017](#_bookmark26)). The increase in the intensity of carboxylic acid/ester peaks and the presence of ketone group peaks in the spectra confirmed that TYL is adsorbed on CCM-AC.

- 1.  _Batch adsorption experiment_
        1. _Eﬀect of dosage_

The effect of CCM-AC dosage on CCM-AC adsorption is shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark4)a. 0.08 g CCM-AC and 50 mL TYL (10 mg L−1) solution are adopted in subsequent experiments for suitable removal rate and the adsorption capacity.

- -   1.  _The eﬀect of pH_

To better understand about the adsorption mechanism of TYL on CCM-AC, the adsorption capacity of CCM-AC for TYL and the zeta po-tential of CCM-AC at different pH are shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark4)b. As the pH in-creased from 3.0 to 7.0, the adsorption capacity increased from 37.94 to

56.56 mg g−1, when pH increased from 7.0 to 11.0, the adsorption capacity dropped to 44.9 mg g−1. In addition, with the increase of pH, the ζ potential of CCM-AC gradually decreased from 19.2 to −20.1 mV,

the iso-electric points (IEPs) of CCM-AC is 7.2.

The IEPs of TYL is 7.1. When the pH of the solution is lower than 7.1, the positively charged TYL+ becomes the main ionic form; when the pH of the solution is greater than 7.1, the uncharged molecular TYL° accounts for the majority ([Lu, Jiang, Wang, Wang, & Yang, 2013](#_bookmark29)). At pH lower than 7, both CCM-AC and TYL are positively surface charged. Despite the charge repulsion between CCM-AC and TYL, TYL is still adsorbed by CCM-AC. According to the analysis of the FTIR and XPS data, the carboxyl group and many hydroxyl groups exist on the surface of the adsorbent CCM-AC, which is favorable for the aﬃnity adsorption to the hydroxyl group. The molecule of TYL contains several hydrogen bonds that can act as hydrogen acceptors or donors ([Guo et al., 2013](#_bookmark21)). Under acidic conditions, H-bond between TYL and the CCM-AC func-tional group (eOH) may be the main interaction of TYL with CCM-AC adsorption ([Liu, Zhong, Zhao, Frear, & Zheng, 2015](#_bookmark28)). When the pH of

the solution increases, the π–π EDA interaction between the strong

electron-withdrawing ketone group on the TYL and the adsorbent is the main interaction ([Guo et al., 2016](#_bookmark20)).

- -   1.  _Adsorption kinetics study_

The results of adsorption kinetics of TYL is displayed in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark5). The adsorption of TYL by CCM-AC is faster in the first three hours, then slows down until reaches the adsorption equilibrium in about eight hours, the _qe,_max of CCM-AC is 59.26 mg g−1, which is superior to other adsorbents system (Table S3). The pseudo-first-order kinetic, pseudo-second-order kinetic, and intra-particle diffusion models ([Luo et al.,](#_bookmark30) [2016](#_bookmark30)) are used to discuss the adsorption kinetics of TYL on CCM-AC to explore the mechanism of controlling the adsorption process, the cal-culation formulas for these three models are listed in the support in-formation. The kinetic parameters and the results are listed in [Table 1](#_bookmark6). The _r2_ of the pseudo-first-order and pseudo-second-order kinetic models are all high, reaching to 0.99. This indicates that the adsorption of TYL

- -   1.  _Eﬀect of bed height of fixed-bed_

Breakthrough curves for TYL adsorption under different _H_ (2, 3 and 5 cm) are presented in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)a. As the H increased from 2 to 5 cm, the _ts_

on CCM-AC is a complex process controlled by both physical interac-tions and chemical interactions.

The kinetic data is analyzed by using the intraparticle diffusion model to explore the position of particles during intra-diffusion in the adsorption process. The model curve ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark5) (right)) does not pass through the origin and showed significant transition, indicating that the effects of surface adsorption and intra-particle diffusion on the ad-sorption process are not negligible. Therefore, the adsorption of TYL on CCM-AC can be divided into three stages: The first stage is the ad-sorption of TYL through the solution to the outer surface of CCM-AC; the second stage is gradual adsorption controlled by intra-granular diffusion; The intra-particle diffusion rate in the third stage is sig-nificantly lower than in the previous stage because the molecules of TYL are larger and the diffusion of micro-pores is diﬃcult ([Lu et al., 2013](#_bookmark29)).

- -   1.  _Adsorption isotherms study_

Fig. S1 shows the adsorption isotherms of TYL at 298 K, 303 K and 313 K. Table S4 lists the calculated parameters of the and their re-gression coeﬃcients for Langmuir and Freundlich models. Adsorption isotherms show that the adsorption data is better align with the Langmuir isotherm model, which indicates that TYL adsorption on CCM-AC is the monolayer sorption.

- 1.  _Fixed-bed column adsorption experiments_

Bed height (_H_), inlet solution flow rate (_Q_), initial concentration (_C0_) and pH are four important factors of the fixed-bed column system. In order to evaluate the adsorption performances of the column ad-sorption system, the outlet concentration/inlet concentration (_Ct/C0_) was set to 0.1 as the breakthrough point, _Ct/C0_ \= 0.9 was set as the saturation point, and the breakthrough curves under different

and _Vs_ of the column adsorption system increased from 526 min and 2630 mL to 736 min and 3680 mL, respectively. The breakthrough curve becomes flat, which may result from that the increase in the height of the fixed-bed provides a larger MTZ. This indicates that the increase in the length of the fix-bed column increases the mass of the CCM-AC and the number of adsorption sites in the column adsorption system, allowing the adsorbent to take longer to reach saturation. In addition, the higher _ts_ means that the TYL can diffuse suﬃciently into the pores of CCM-AC, so the _RS_ increased from 40.73% to 51.81% as the _H_ increased. The high _H_ was beneficial to antibiotics adsorption.

- -   1.  _Eﬀect of flow rate of TYL_

[Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)b shows the effect of _Q_ on the TYL adsorption performances of a column packed with CCM-AC. As _Q_ increased from 4 to 6 mL min−1, the _ts_ of the column adsorption system decreased from 620 to

446.67 min, while the _Vs_ increased from 2480 to 2680 mL. Further-more, the breakthrough curve moves toward the left and the slope becomes larger ([Darweesh & Ahmed, 2017](#_bookmark16)). This may be due to a de-crease in the interaction between TYL and CCM-AC at higher _Q_. The slower _R_ provides a longer residence time for TYL and allows it to be in full contact with the adsorbate so that more of the adsorbate's adsorp-tion site is occupied by TYL, resulting in an increase in the total removal rate and _qe_ of the TYL. Thus, lower _R_ is beneficial to the adsorption progress.

- -   1.  _Eﬀect of inlet concentration of TYL_

The effect of _C0_ of TYL on the adsorption performances of columns packed with CCM-AC is shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)c. The larger _C0_ resulted in a greater impelling force for the mass transfer of TYL and hence the CCM-AC achieved saturation more quickly. Likewise, the breakthrough curves were steeper as influent solution concentration increased, which indicated a relative smaller MTZ and intra-particle diffusion dominated

Fig. 6. Breakthrough curves of TYL removal by CCM-AC using fixed-bed columns of (a) different heights of bed, (b) different flow rates, (c) different initial concentrations, and (d) different pH.

the adsorption process ([Liao et al., 2013](#_bookmark27)). The adsorption sites saturated faster in the column at higher _C0_ ([Radhika et al., 2018](#_bookmark36)). When the _C0_ was increased from 5 to 15 mg L−1, the _ts_ and _VS_ decreased from 776 min and 3880 mL to 308 min and 1540 mL, respectively. The re-duction in _ts_ leaves the internal and external active sites of adsorbent do not have enough time to capture TYL, which may lead to a decrease in the overall removal rate. Accordingly, TYL adsorption is more favorable in lower _C0_.

- -   1.  _Eﬀect of pH of TYL solution_

The effect of pH value of TYL solution on the adsorption perfor-mances of CCM-AC packed column is shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark7)d. When the pH value is 3.0 and 11.0, _tb_, _ts_ and _qs_ are greatly reduced, and the break-through curve became steep. TYL exists in a protonated state at low pH. Similarly, the surface of CCM-AC is positively charged at low pH. There are electrostatic repulsions between TYL and CCM-AC, which hinders the adsorption of TYL by CCM-AC. The pH of the solution is a very

important factor for the adsorption process, affecting the breakthrough curve and the adsorption performances.

- -   1.  _Dynamic adsorption model_

The predicted and experimental breakthrough curves of TYL ad-sorption by CCM-AC under different influencing factors are summarized in Fig. S2. And the calculated parameters of the Adams-Bohart, Thomas, Yoon-Nelson, BDST and Dose Response models are summed up in [Table 3](#_bookmark9). For the _H_, _Q_, and _C0_, the correlation coeﬃcients for these five models ranged from 0.9713 to 0.9934, indicating that these five models can better predict the breakthrough curves under these three variables. The Dose Response model may be closer to the actual situation.

The Adams-Bohart and BDST models have the same effect, the _k_ value increases with increasing _Q_, at the same time, the _N0_ value de-creases. For the Thomas models, the _q0_ decreased when _Q_ increased, which agreed with experimental results. - -   1.  _Regeneration experiment_

The regenerated CCM-AC was reused in subsequent adsorption ex-periments (conditions as in [Table 2](#_bookmark8), number 1) and the adsorption-desorption-suction process was repeated for five cycles. The adsorption breakthrough curve and desorption curve of CCM-AC on TYL (Fig. S3) showed that the adsorption capacity decreased, indicating that some of the active sites were non-renewable. After 5 cycles, the saturated ad-sorption of CCM-AC to TYL still had 36.63%, which may be caused by the tight combination of TYL and adsorbent ([Guo et al., 2018](#_bookmark22)).

- 1.  _Adsorption mechanism analysis_

Adsorption mechanism of TYL on CCM-AC and the structure of TYL are shown in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark10). The adsorption of TYL is complex and is mainly controlled by the following adsorption mechanisms:

(1) H-bonding: FTIR, XPS spectrum shows that plenty of hydroxyl and carboxyl groups exist on the surface of CCM-AC, which is beneficial to the occurrence of hydrogen bonding. (2) Electrostatic interaction: The zeta potential of CCM-AC indicates that its IEPs are 7.2. When the pH is lower than 7.2, the electrostatic repulsion of CCM-AC and TYL+

affects the adsorption. (3) π-π EDA interaction: It is obtained in the

analysis of the influence of pH on the adsorption effect. Under acidic conditions, the adsorption mechanism is mostly controlled by (1) and

(2). Under neutral and alkaline conditions, π-π EDA action and H bond

action control the adsorption process. (4) Internal diffusion: The ad-sorption kinetics indicates that the adsorption process is consistent with

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 7. The scheme for fabrication CCM-AC and the adsorption mechanism of TYL on CCM-AC.

internal diffusion. (5) Size-exclusion effect: The kinetic data analysis showed that the adsorption of TYL on CCM-AC is a slow process. The BET results show that the average pore size of CCM-AC is 23.844 nm, which is a mesoporous adsorbent. TYL is a non-rigid molecule with a large and flexible structure ([Ji et al., 2010](#_bookmark24)). Therefore, TYL adsorption by CCM-AC is affected by the size-exclusion effect, and it slowly diffuses in the pores of the adsorbents.

1. Conclusions

Chitosan/cellulose nanocomposite adsorbents entrapped with AC with porous networks structure were successfully prepared by a sol-gel phase inversion method. The adsorbents had high adsorption eﬃciency for low concentration TYL. SEM, BET and porosity analysis indicated that the microspheres had a multi-layered pore structure. Analysis of FTIR, XPS, Zeta potential and the effect of pH on adsorption showed

that H-bond interaction, electrostatic interaction and π-π EDA inter-action played the important role in adsorption process. In the batch

adsorption experiment, the _qe,max_ of CCM-AC was 59.26 mg g−1, the size-exclusion effect affects the rate of adsorption. The nonlinearity of the adsorption curve was significant and was consistent with the in-ternal diffusion characteristics. Column adsorption experiments have shown that the breakthrough data fitted better with the Dose Response model. The fixed-bed column adsorption system showed a good ability to continuously treat water. Regeneration experiment shown the design adsorbents had good usability. Based on the comprehensive under-standing of the adsorption mechanism, chitosan and cellulose, and AC are very suitable for using as biological aﬃnity carrier and functional filler to design adsorbents to control antibiotic pollution.
